title: Scheherazade's Thousand Nights
text:
King Shahryar discovered that his wife had betrayed him, and the shock turned him cruel. He had her executed, and then decided that no woman could be trusted. Every day he married a young woman, and every morning he had her put to death. Families fled the city with their daughters, and fear spread through the kingdom.

Shahrazad, the clever and well read daughter of the king's vizier, told her father she would marry the king. He begged her not to, but she had a plan. On her wedding night she arranged for her younger sister, Dunyazad, to be brought to the room and to ask her for a story.

Shahrazad began a tale, and the king listened. When dawn broke, the story was not finished, and she stopped. It was nothing, she said, compared with what she could tell the next night, if the king let her live. He wanted to hear the end, so he spared her for one more day.

The next night she finished that story and began another, which also broke off at dawn. So it went on, night after night, with tales nested inside tales, for a thousand and one nights. By the end, the king had changed. He gave up his vow, and Shahrazad became his queen.
lesson: When you cannot win an argument head on, change the situation one step at a time. Keeping the other side curious about what comes next buys time for minds to change.
location: Medieval Middle East (Persian and Arabic tradition)
source: One Thousand and One Nights, frame story
caveat: Endings differ between manuscripts and editions; in some, Shahrazad has borne the king children by the end.
